en: Majjhima Nikāya 3:
Dhammadāyādasutta.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.”
"I have compassion for you:
'How may my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things?
But if you, monks, were to be heirs to material things and not heirs to the Dhamma, you would thereby be taking hold of me."
‘The Teacher’s disciples dwell as heirs to material things, not as heirs to the Dhamma’—
I too would be included in that:
‘The Teacher’s disciples dwell as heirs to material things, not as heirs to the Dhamma.’
"And you, monks, should be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things; and you should not be attached to that thought:
'The Teacher's disciples dwell as heirs in the Dhamma, not as heirs in material things';
nor should I be attached to that thought."
‘The Teacher’s disciples dwell as heirs to the Dhamma, not as heirs to material things.
Therefore, monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.
I have compassion for you.
‘How might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things?
In this case, monks, I might have finished eating, been invited to stop, being fully satisfied, having completed my meal and had enough;
yet there might be almsfood remaining for me that is fit to be discarded.
Then two monks might come, overcome by hunger and weakness.
To them I would say:
"Monks, I have already eaten, I have been invited, I am full, finished, satiated, and have had enough."
"I have this alms-food, which is an extra item and something that should be discarded.
If you wish, eat it; if you do not eat it, I shall now discard it on ground with little vegetation, or I shall throw it into water where there are no living beings.
Then, a certain monk might think thus:
“The Blessed One has finished his meal, has been invited to stop, is fully satisfied, has eaten his fill, and has had enough.
Yet there is this alms-food remaining for the Blessed One, which is of a nature to be discarded.
If we do not eat it, the Blessed One will now either discard it on ground where there is no vegetation or throw it into water where there are no living beings.”
Furthermore, this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.
Now, that which is called almsfood is indeed a material thing.
‘What if I were to pass this day and night without eating even this almsfood, but rather by means of this very hunger and weakness?
He would then pass that day and night without eating that almsfood, but rather by means of that very hunger and weakness.
Then, a second bhikkhu might think:
“The Blessed One has finished his meal, has been invited to stop, is fully satisfied, has had enough, and has eaten his fill.
Yet there is this alms-food remaining for the Blessed One, which is of a nature to be discarded.
If we do not eat it, the Blessed One will now either discard it on ground with no greenery or throw it into water containing no living beings.”
‘What if, having eaten this almsfood and dispelled my hunger and weakness, I were to pass this day and night in this way?
Then, having eaten that almsfood and dispelled his hunger and weakness, he would pass that day and night in this way.
Even though, monks, that bhikkhu has eaten that almsfood and dispelled his hunger and weakness...
In this way he would spend that day and night; yet, even so, that first monk of mine would still be more worthy of honor and more praiseworthy. Why is that?
Because, monks, for that monk it will lead to long-term fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, easy support, and the arousal of energy.
"Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.
I have compassion for you:
'How may my disciples be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things?'"
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
There, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, monks. The monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta,
“Friend,” and the Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“In what way, friends, do the disciples of a teacher who dwells in seclusion fail to train in seclusion, and in what way do the disciples of a teacher who dwells in seclusion train in seclusion?
“Friends, we come from afar to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sāriputta.
It would be well if the Venerable Sāriputta himself were to clarify the meaning of this statement.”
“Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will retain it.
“Therefore, friends, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"To what extent, friends, do disciples not train in seclusion when the Teacher dwells in seclusion?
In this case, friends, disciples do not train in seclusion while the Teacher dwells in seclusion."
And as for those things which the Teacher has declared should be abandoned, they do not abandon those things;
they are luxurious, lax, leaders in backsliding, and have cast off the burden of seclusion.
In this regard, friends, the elder bhikkhus are to be censured on three grounds.
‘While the Teacher dwells in seclusion, his disciples do not train in seclusion’— on account of this first ground,

elder bhikkhus become subject to censure. ‘They do not abandon those qualities for which the Teacher has declared their abandonment’— on account of this second ground, elder bhikkhus become subject to censure.
For this second reason, the elder bhikkhus are to be censured.
“They are luxurious, they are lax, they are leaders in backsliding, and they have abandoned the burden of solitude”—
for this third reason, the elder bhikkhus are to be censured.
Venerable friends, elder bhikkhus are censurable on these three grounds.
In this regard, venerable friends, middle-ranking bhikkhus...
[and] new bhikkhus are censurable on three grounds.
‘While the Teacher dwells in seclusion, his disciples do not train in seclusion’—
by this first ground, new bhikkhus become objects of reproach.
‘They do not abandon those qualities for which the Teacher has declared their abandonment’— by this second ground, new bhikkhus become objects of reproach.
For this second reason, new bhikkhus are to be censured.
"They are luxurious, they are lax, they are pioneers in backsliding, and they have abandoned the burden of solitude"—
for this third reason, new bhikkhus are to be censured.
"Friends, new bhikkhus are to be censured for three reasons.
To this extent, friends, disciples do not train in seclusion when the Teacher dwells in seclusion.
But to what extent, friends, do disciples train in seclusion when the Teacher dwells in seclusion?"
In this case, friends, while the Teacher dwells in seclusion, his disciples train themselves in seclusion:
they abandon those qualities which the Teacher has said should be abandoned;
they do not become luxurious or lax, nor do they cast off the yoke of spiritual decline, but rather take the lead in seclusion.
In this regard, friends, elder bhikkhus are praiseworthy for three reasons.
"The disciples of the Teacher, who dwells in seclusion, train themselves in seclusion"—
this is the first reason for which elder bhikkhus are praiseworthy.
‘They abandon those qualities which the Teacher has declared should be abandoned’—by this second ground, the elder bhikkhus become praiseworthy.
‘They are neither luxurious nor lax; having laid aside the burden of worldly descent, they are leaders in seclusion.’
By this third ground, elder bhikkhus become praiseworthy.
Friends, by these three grounds, elder bhikkhus become praiseworthy.
In that regard, friends, as for the middle bhikkhus... [and so forth].
New bhikkhus are praiseworthy for three reasons.
"The disciples of the Teacher, who dwells in seclusion, train themselves in seclusion"—
this is the first reason for which new bhikkhus are praiseworthy.
‘They abandon those things which the Teacher has declared should be abandoned’—by this second ground, new bhikkhus become worthy of praise.
‘They are not luxurious, nor lax; they have laid aside the burden of falling back into worldly ways and are leaders in solitude.’
By this third ground, new bhikkhus become praiseworthy.
New bhikkhus, friends, are praiseworthy by these three grounds.
To this extent, friends, disciples train in seclusion following the Teacher who dwells in seclusion.
In this regard, friends, greed is evil and hatred is evil.
For the abandoning of greed and for the abandoning of hatred, there is a middle way that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And what, friends, is that middle way which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna?
This very Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, friends, is that Middle Way which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to Nibbāna.
In this regard, friends, anger is evil and resentment is evil; ...pe...
slander is evil and insolence is evil;
envy is evil and stinginess is evil.
Deceit is evil and guile is evil;
stubbornness is evil and hostility is evil;
conceit is evil and arrogance is evil.
Intoxication is evil, and negligence is evil.

For the abandoning of intoxication and for the abandoning of negligence, there is the Middle Way that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And what, friends, is that Middle Way that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna?
"This very Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, friends, is that Middle Way which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna."
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta.
The monks were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta.
The third discourse, "The Heirs of the Dhamma," is concluded.
